lead: Every body has weight, and that weight can be treated as one force acting at a single point: the centre of gravity. For a thin wire or a flat plate, the same averaging idea gives a purely geometric point, the centroid. Engineers use it to balance shafts, place lifting hooks, check that a crane will not tip, and locate the centroid of a composite beam section. The centroid is a weighted average of positions: weight by length for a line, by area for a surface. This chapter sets up that average and the standard results you should know.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for the idea of a force as a vector with a line of action, and first-year integration for the element dA.

sections.h3: Centre of gravity, centre of mass, centroid

blocks.text: Every small piece of a body has a weight ΔW. The total weight W is the sum of those small weights: W = Σ ΔW. In 4.2 this sum becomes an integral. The line of action of the total weight passes through one point, the centre of gravity G. If the gravitational field g (in N/kg) is the same at every point of the body, the total weight acts through the centre of mass, so G and the centre of mass are the same point. Density need not be uniform for this. For a thin wire or a flat plate of uniform density, density cancels out and the point depends only on shape. That geometric point is the centroid. Some syllabi call it the centre of area.
x̄ = Σ x dA / A,   ȳ = Σ y dA / A
blocks.where: x̄ and ȳ are the centroid coordinates in mm; x and y are the coordinates of the element dA in mm; dA is the element area in mm²; A is the total area in mm²; Σ means sum over all elements.

blocks.text: Multiply both sides by A: A x̄ = Σ x dA. The quantity A x̄ is the first moment of area about the y-axis, written Qy. Its unit is mm² × mm = mm³. For a line, replace area by length: L x̄ = Σ x dL. This is the first moment of length about the y-axis, unit mm × mm = mm².
A x̄ = Σ x dA = Q<sub>y</sub>
blocks.where: Q<sub>y</sub> is the first moment of area about the y-axis in mm³; A is area in mm²; x̄ is the centroid's x-coordinate in mm.

blocks.text: Symmetry saves work. If a figure has one axis of symmetry, the centroid lies on that axis. If it has two axes of symmetry, the centroid is at their intersection. The move from summing elements to integrating them is in 4.2.

Learn three standard results. A straight line of length L has its centroid at the midpoint. A semicircular arc of radius r has its centroid on the axis of symmetry at distance 2r/π from the centre. For r = 50 mm, that is 31.8 mm. A quarter-circular arc of radius r has its centroid at 2r/π from each of the two radii that form its ends.

These three are centroids of lines. For areas, a triangular area has its centroid on the median at h/3 from the base and 2h/3 from the apex, where h is the triangle height. A semicircular area has its centroid at 4r/3π from the centre, a different point; only a few syllabi need it in this chapter. The second moment of area, which measures spread rather than balance, starts in 4.4.
Worked example 1 below bends a uniform wire into an L and finds its centroid step by step.

examples.question: A uniform wire is bent into an L. A 300 mm length lies along the x-axis from (0, 0) to (300, 0). A 400 mm length stands vertically from (300, 0) to (300, 400). All lengths are in mm. Find the centroid of the wire.
steps: Segment 1 is the horizontal piece: L<sub>1</sub> = 300 mm, centroid (x<sub>1</sub>, y<sub>1</sub>) = (150, 0) mm.
Segment 2 is the vertical piece: L<sub>2</sub> = 400 mm, centroid (x<sub>2</sub>, y<sub>2</sub>) = (300, 200) mm.
The centroid is (235.7, 114.3) mm. It lies outside the wire itself, which is normal for a bent line.
examples.answer: The centroid of the L-shaped wire is at x̄ = 235.7 mm and ȳ = 114.3 mm.

traps: Weighting by the wrong quantity: length for a wire, area for a plate, volume for a solid. The formula changes with the element.
Forgetting that a hole carries a negative area or negative volume in the sum, so its moment is subtracted.
Using 4r/3π for a semicircular arc. The arc centroid is 2r/π from the centre; 4r/3π belongs to a semicircular area.
Mixing units of first moment: area first moment is mm³, line first moment is mm².
Assuming the centroid must lie inside the material. An L-shaped wire, a ring and a horse-shoe all have centroids outside the body.

quiz.q: Define the centroid of a plane area.
quiz.a: The centroid is the geometric point (x̄, ȳ) where x̄ = Σ x dA / A and ȳ = Σ y dA / A; it depends only on the shape, not on density.

quiz.q: What is the unit of the first moment of area about the y-axis?
quiz.a: mm³, because it is area in mm² multiplied by a coordinate in mm.

quiz.q: Why can the centroid of a bent wire lie outside the wire?
quiz.a: The centroid is a weighted average of the positions of all elements. No element needs to sit at that average position, so the balance point can be off the material.

quiz.q: A wire has a 200 mm straight piece along the x-axis from (0, 0) to (200, 0) and a 200 mm straight piece from (200, 0) to (200, 200). All lengths in mm. Find the centroid.
Find the centroid distance from the centre for a semicircular arc of radius 50 mm.
quiz.a: Distance = 2r/π = 2×50/π = 31.8 mm from the centre, on the axis of symmetry.

quiz.q: A flat figure has one axis of symmetry but no second axis. What can you say about its centroid, and what remains unknown?
quiz.a: The centroid lies somewhere on the axis of symmetry, so one coordinate is fixed. The position along that axis still needs a moment calculation.

quiz.q: A rectangular plate has a circular hole. How should the hole be handled in the centroid calculation?
quiz.a: Treat the hole as negative area: subtract its area and subtract its first moment from the solid plate's totals. The centroid shifts away from the hole.

beyond: Not for the exam. In machine design, the centroid of a weld group or a bolt pattern sets the load share per bolt, and in civil engineering the centroid of a bridge deck section decides how much it twists under eccentric load. Robotics uses centre of mass in balance controllers for legged robots. Search next for centroid of a weld group, centre of mass of a human body segment, and first moment of area plastic section modulus.
